title: JD.com acquires Ceconomy to expand EU logistics
metaDescription: JD.com takes over MediaMarkt and Saturn owner Ceconomy. Hong Kong reviews river fees to fight mainland port competition. MSC expands Shikra service.
bottomLine: JD.com now owns a massive European retail and warehouse network via Ceconomy, but must open its logistics to rivals for 10 years. Hong Kong is cutting river fees to stop cargo leaking to Shenzhen and Guangzhou.

stories.headline: JD.com takes over Ceconomy to build European footprint
stories.tldr: The European Commission approved JD.com's acquisition of Ceconomy, provided JD.com opens its logistics services to third-party retailers for 10 years.
stories.whatHappened:
The European Commission approved JD.com's takeover of Ceconomy, which owns MediaMarkt and Saturn. Ceconomy generated 22.4 billion euros in revenue last fiscal year. The Commission found JD.com received Chinese state subsidies in the form of grants, tax incentives, and preferential financing to build its technical and logistical capacities.

To prevent market distortion, the Commission imposed conditions on the deal. JD.com must provide its warehousing, logistics, and technological services to third-party retailers under the same terms as Ceconomy. This agreement lasts for ten years and the Commission will monitor implementation.
stories.whyItMatters:
If you are a high-volume seller shipping electronics or home goods into Europe, this changes your options. JD.com is not just buying stores, it is buying a physical retail and warehouse network to bypass the cooling Chinese domestic market. The forced open-access rule is the key for you. You may soon be able to plug into JD.com's high-efficiency logistics and warehousing across Europe without being a JD.com partner.

For sellers using FBA or local 3PLs in Germany and surrounding markets, this introduces a massive new competitor with deep Chinese state-backed pockets. Expect aggressive pricing on fulfilment and warehousing as JD.com tries to scale its European operations. If you source from China and sell in the EU, your landed cost could drop if you shift to JD.com's open-access network once it goes live.
stories.hotTake: JD.com is playing the long game. They are buying their way into the EU to hedge against China's slowing growth. The open-access condition is a small price to pay for a ready-made network of stores and warehouses. I expect them to undercut every European 3PL on price to win market share.
actions: Map your current EU warehousing costs against JD.com's existing China-to-EU rates
Wait for the open-access API documentation to see if you can integrate your Shopify or TikTok store

stories.headline: Hong Kong reviews river fees to stop cargo loss to mainland
stories.tldr: Hong Kong is reviewing permit fees for river trade vessels to remain competitive against ports in Shenzhen and Guangzhou.
stories.whatHappened:
Secretary for transport and logistics Chan Mei-po announced a review of permit fees charged to river trade vessels. The move follows increasing competition from mainland Chinese terminals in Shenzhen and Guangzhou. 

China-flagged vessels currently move containers between the Pearl River Delta and Hong Kong for transfer to ocean-going ships. The Hong Kong government aims to maintain port competitiveness by adjusting these costs to stop cargo from bypassing the city entirely in favour of mainland terminals.
stories.whyItMatters:
If you use Hong Kong as a transhipment hub for goods coming out of the Pearl River Delta, your feeder costs are about to change. Many operators have already shifted to Shenzhen or Guangzhou to avoid the bureaucracy and fees of the Hong Kong river trade. 

For the seller who still relies on HK for specific banking or customs reasons, a drop in these fees makes the route more viable. However, if you have already moved your operations to Shenzhen, do not rush back. The mainland ports have already won the efficiency war. This is a defensive move by Hong Kong, not a structural improvement in how they handle containers. Watch your forwarder's quotes for the PRD-to-HK leg over the next month.
stories.hotTake: Hong Kong is too late. Once a supply chain shifts to Shenzhen or Guangzhou for speed and cost, it stays there. Lowering fees is a band-aid on a broken leg. I would stick with mainland terminals unless you have a specific regulatory need for HK.
actions: Ask your forwarder if they have seen a shift in river trade pricing for the PRD lane
Compare your current Shenzhen port fees against the updated HK river permit costs

stories.headline: MSC expands Shikra service to UAE and Oman
stories.tldr: MSC added calls at Khor Fakkan in the UAE and Sohar in Oman to its Far East-India Shikra service.
stories.whatHappened:
MSC extended its Shikra service, which connects major Chinese ports and Singapore to India, into the Middle East. The service now includes direct calls at Khor Fakkan in the UAE and Sohar in Oman. 

MSC is increasing the vessel deployment for the Shikra service to 15 containerships. These ships have varying capacities and will provide a direct link between Chinese manufacturing hubs and the Gulf region.
stories.whyItMatters:
If you are expanding your sales into the Middle East, you now have a more direct sea-freight option from China. Previously, many shipments to the UAE or Oman required multiple transhipments, which added 7 to 14 days to your lead time and increased the risk of damage or loss.

Direct calls at Khor Fakkan and Sohar reduce the handling of your containers. For sellers of bulky goods or electronics shipping to the Gulf, this means lower risk and potentially lower freight rates due to the increased capacity of 15 ships on the lane. If you use a 3PL in Dubai or Muscat, ask them to check MSC Shikra schedules to see if you can shave a week off your transit time.
stories.hotTake: The Middle East is the new growth frontier for Chinese exporters. MSC knows this. They are adding capacity before the rush. If you are still shipping to the UAE via indirect routes, you are wasting money and time.
actions: Request a quote for the China-to-Sohar direct lane from your carrier
Update your lead time estimates for UAE-bound stock to reflect the direct Shikra service

faq.question: Can I use JD.com logistics to ship my goods in Europe?
faq.answer: Yes, eventually. The European Commission approved JD.com's takeover of Ceconomy on the condition that JD.com provides its warehousing and logistics services to third-party retailers for 10 years. You will need to wait for JD.com to open its API and service agreements to non-Ceconomy partners, but the legal requirement is now in place.

faq.question: Is it cheaper to ship via Hong Kong or Shenzhen right now?
faq.answer: Shenzhen and Guangzhou are generally cheaper and faster. Hong Kong is currently reviewing its river trade permit fees because it is losing too much cargo to the mainland. Unless you have a specific reason to use HK, mainland terminals offer better integration with factories in the Pearl River Delta.

faq.question: How do I get my stock from China to the UAE faster?
faq.answer: Use the MSC Shikra service. MSC has extended this service to include direct calls at Khor Fakkan in the UAE and Sohar in Oman. This removes the need for multiple transhipments and uses a fleet of 15 ships to maintain connectivity between major Chinese ports and the Gulf.
